title: London police counter Mario Hamel, who hanged himself in custody in November 2010, was the `author of his own misfortune?
article: The family of a London man who killed himself in an un-monitored and unchecked holding cell is suing police for $5.3 million, claiming officers' verbal and physical abuse fed the mental anguish that led to the suicide.
In response, London police say Mario Hamel was "the author of his own misfortune."

The harsh claims of competing legal actions - none of them proven in court - surfaced on the same day London police revealed improvements to its cell checks in response to the recommendations of an inquest into Hamel's death.
The changes provided small comfort to the man's widow, her lawyer Evelyn ten Cate said Thursday.
"What she said was, 'That's all fine but it's never going to bring him back.' She's devastated by the loss of her husband. But she is hopeful the recommendations will prevent another tragedy."
He woke up at 2:52 a.m. the next day and spent 11 minutes in an eventually successful effort to hang himself in a police holding cell.
His suicide was visible on a monitor, but no one was watching the screen at the time, the inquest heard in January.
The inquest also heard that police forgot Hamel was in their cells and failed to check on him in the minutes after his death.
Those bare bones of the story that came out during the inquest are not in dispute, but the competing legal actions add contradictory and startling claims about the details of the night in question.
Hamel's family say the arresting officers became increasingly frustrated because of the man's lack of English.
Instead of contacting an officer who could speak French, they "unlawfully detained (him) by aggressively grabbing his arms behind his back" and handcuffing him, the statement says.
Hamel begged the handcuffs be taken off, and his wife pleaded with the officers not to take him because he was terrified of jail.
Police ignored the complaints, neglected to investigate Hamel's emotional or physical state, and took him away without explanation, the lawsuit says.
"Mario was forcibly removed from his home, in front of his family, without a jacket or even shoes on his feet," it says.

Officers named in the lawsuit physically assaulted and "verbally attacked and degraded" Hamel while in custody, "contributing to the mental anguish . . . and Mario's decision to hang himself," the lawsuit claims.
Chief Brad Duncan and the police board were negligent in their training, supervision and assessment of their officers, and in their operation of the holding cell area, the lawsuit claims.
The lawsuit claims family members continue to suffer from anxiety, depression and other physical and mental conditions from Hamel's death.
In the statement of defence, police say Hamel was drunk and agitated, and ignored the directions of arresting officers although he understood what they were saying.
Officers knew Hamel had been arrested before at the same house, and had earlier been under an order - no longer in effect - not to communicate with his wife.
The arresting officers learned from his wife the couple was in the process of separating and lived in separate quarters in the house. His stepchildren wanted police to remove him from the house.
Hamel tried to explain how he had touched his daughter's cheek that night by touching the officers. At that point, he was handcuffed.
Officers arrested Hamel at 12:57 a.m. Nov. 25 and took him to the police station because they were worried what might happen if he stayed in the house that night, the statement of defence says.
Hamel understood and didn't object to going to the station for a few hours to sober up in time to head to work that morning, the statement of defence says.
Hamel didn't show any signs that he was at risk of hurting himself, the statement of defence says.
